title: Incremental-merge batching + KV-aware eviction heuristic for low-latency streaming chat
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background:
Streaming chat workloads require sub-100ms tail latencies for first tokens while also achieving high token throughput for long-running sessions. Existing continuous batching approaches either prioritize latency (small micro-batches) or throughput (large merges) but do not jointly optimize for KV cache pressure and GPU memory fragmentation that arise from variable-length chat sessions.

Goal:
Design and prototype a batch-formation heuristic that: (1) returns low-latency first tokens for streaming chat, (2) incrementally merges compatible micro-batches to increase GPU throughput, and (3) manages KV cache slots to limit GPU memory spike and fragmentation without hurting sequence re-use hit-rate.

Proposed approach (Incremental-Merge + KV-Aware Eviction):
1) Dual-queue intake: new streaming requests enter a "fast-path" micro-queue (max micro-batch size=4, wait cap=12ms) to guarantee low P95/P99 for first tokens. Compatible micro-batches are tracked for affinity (model variant, sequence-length bucket, quantization profile).
2) Incremental merge window: micro-batches that remain in the fast-path for >12ms are eligible for merge into a merged-batch queue. The merge attempts to align KV cache layout to minimize slot shuffling: sessions with high reuse score are placed together.
3) KV-weighted-slotting: assign each session a reuse score computed from historical prefix reuse and session age; eviction priority = (age * 0.3) + (1 - reuse_score) * 0.7. This biases eviction towards stale sessions with low reuse while protecting hot conversational sessions.
4) GPU scratch reserve: maintain a small reserved slab per GPU (configurable, default 256MB) for transient KV growth during merges to avoid OOM spikes. If the reserve is exhausted, the merge is throttled and fallbacks trigger (spill oldest low-reuse KV page to CPU async or split merged batch).
5) Compact KV layout: use 16-bit index compaction and on-the-fly sparse packing for cached KV blocks to reduce per-session overhead. Combined with FP16 keys, this reduces KV resident memory by ~18-25% in early experiments.

Trade-offs considered:
- Aggressive merging improves throughput but risks increasing first-token latency for subsequent micro-batches. The dual-queue + time cap balances this.
- Protecting hot sessions reduces eviction churn but can increase memory pressure; we counter with async spill and reserved slab.
- Compacting KV structures adds CPU work during packing/unpacking; benchmark suggests cost is offset by lowered GPU memory pressure and fewer merges aborted due to OOM.

Experiments & results (prototype on dev cluster):
- Workload: 1200 concurrent streaming sessions with geometric distribution of lengths (mean 600 tokens), mixed model variants (chat-1.4/2.0).
- Baseline (current continuous batcher): P50=22ms, P95=210ms, average throughput=48k tokens/s, KV resident per-GPU=34GB.
- Incremental-Merge + KV-aware eviction (alpha): P50=24ms, P95=130ms, average throughput=62k tokens/s, KV resident per-GPU=27GB.
- Observations: P95 improved substantially (fewer merged-induced tail spikes), throughput increased ~29%, and memory footprint reduced ~20%. Some CPU overhead observed (~8% increase in host CPU during compaction phases).

Open design decisions:
- Affinity scoring: how to weight model variant vs seq-length vs quantization profile when merging. Current alpha weights model_variant higher; need to run ablation.
- Eviction cooldown: after eviction, a session can be reloaded causing rewarm cost. We need a backoff policy to avoid thrashing.
- Spill strategy: currently async-to-CPU is implemented as a background LRU writer; we should compare with compressed on-GPU paging (if supported by HW).

Acceptance criteria for this ticket:
- Merge heuristic implemented in the runtime prototype with feature flag (incremental_merge_v1).
- End-to-end test harness reproducing benchmark workload and capturing P50/P95/P99 and per-GPU KV resident metrics.
- Documentation of tunable knobs and recommended defaults for dedicated vs hosted tiers.
- One internal PR with implementation and one follow-up PR for perf tests and dashboard.

- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwoodai.com/display/RUNTIME/Incremental-Merge+Batching+Design
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2148
- Perf dashboard (dev cluster): https://dashboards.redwoodai.com/d/rt-incrmerge/streaming-alpha
- Benchmark harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/tree/main/streaming-incmerge

Next steps / Plan:
1) Complete ablation tests for affinity weights (3 days) — Lucas.
2) Implement eviction cooldown and tunable backoff (2 days) — Lucas.
3) Add signal for "spill-readiness" in the KV manager and implement async spill-back refetch path (4 days) — infra pairing with Priya.
4) Safety/perf review and ship feature flag for limited rollout to internal dedicated cluster (runtime-2.3 canary) (5 days) — eng + SRE.

Risks & mitigations:
- OOM during heavy merge bursts: mitigated by GPU scratch reserve and throttling merged-batch creation. Configure automatic rollback on canary if per-GPU utilization > 90% for >5 minutes.
- Increased CPU cost: monitor host CPU and tune compaction frequency; add opt-out flag for hosted customers sensitive to CPU.

Related tickets / background: ENG-12841 (session-aware batch formation), ENG-11563 (dynamic slab prefetch), ENG-10357 (watermark-driven batching).
